title: Macquarie to review KPMG audit process
full_text:
Macquarie chairman Glenn Stevens says the investment banking and asset management giant will review the appointment of KPMG as its auditor, raising the prospect that it could ditch the firm before it starts in the role.
Stevens, a former Reserve Bank of Australia governor, said the Macquarie board had already made "formal inquiries of KPMG" given a stream of departures after senior figures at the auditing firm were caught inappropriately using confidential client files to win contracts with other companies.
Speaking at Macquarie's annual meeting, Stevens said the board was making an "assessment of the integrity of KPMG's pursuit of our audit tender", which would be "supported by an external review" conducted by Allens.
Allens is one of two law firms brought in by KPMG to investigate the allegations about the misuse of confidential client files and other wrongdoing, made by a former employee. KPMG has since said the review by Allens and another by Ashurst had "shortcomings" in their "rigour".
Macquarie has been criticised over how it awarded KPMG the audit contract, one of the most lucrative and coveted among major ASX-listed businesses. Based on an analysis of the latest annual report filed by Macquarie, current auditor PwC earned about $70 million from the company this year, and a further $25 million for auditing funds managed by business.
The Australian Financial Review reported last month that Michelle Hinchliffe, a former senior KPMG partner and now a Macquarie director, had personally attended early-stage bid meetings in Sydney and London as the board worked on who would take over as the company's auditor.
Hinchliffe chairs the Macquarie board's audit committee, which shortlisted only KPMG and PwC to make final pitches. Given PwC had been Macquarie's auditor since 1993, well beyond modern governance limits, KPMG became the only viable choice. It was formally awarded the auditing contract in November last year.
However, KPMG is not due to start auditing Macquarie until April 2028, with the firm's appointment to be put to a vote of investors at next year's annual shareholder meeting.
Stevens has previously described concerns about Hinchliffe's ties to KPMG as "silly talk", adding that she was a "highly credentialled, highly esteemed" member of the board.
Before the annual meeting, CGI Glass Lewis had raised its own concerns, telling clients that investors would need an explanation about how potential conflicts of interest relating to the contract award had been managed.
Glass Lewis, whose recommendations are used by major investors in deciding how to vote on annual meeting resolutions, described Hinchliffe's participation in the decision to appoint KPMG as a "partial recusal" given she was involved in the process but did not vote on the final decision.
On Thursday, Stevens told shareholders that Hinchliffe had "attended the pre-tender period meetings with likely tendering firms on an equal basis across firms, so there were no particular special favours [for] KPMG".
"The board stands behind that. Going forward, we have sought some information from KPMG," Stevens said. "We don't have all of that yet. We probably will have that before too long, but I don't have it today. When we have that, we'll consider what, if anything, further needs to be done."
Peter Nash, another former KPMG partner and the firm's chairman for six years, quit the Westpac board earlier this month, saying his long-term relationship with the accounting giant could create a "perception of bias".
Westpac appointed KPMG as auditor two years ago - the bank said Nash had been excluded on a vote on the contract - but is now considering whether it should re-tender the work after revelations about the misuse of data.
Claims about misconduct made by a former KPMG employee, which have largely been substantiated after several reviews, have led to chair Martin Sheppard's exit and the departure of the firm's chief executive, Andrew Yates, its head of audit, Julian McPherson, and several audit partners.
Stevens told the Macquarie annual meeting on Thursday morning that the company's formal inquiries included whether KPMG had the "ongoing capability to deliver an audit ... given some people have left that firm".
"Serious concerns regarding independence and integrity arose during the pursuit of the Macquarie audit contract," Labor Senator Deborah O'Neill told parliament in March, reading from allegations made by the former KPMG employee. O'Neill alleged in parliament at the time that Hinchliffe "was centrally involved in the Macquarie audit tender process".
O'Neill had written to Macquarie chief executive Shemara Wikramanayake before a parliamentary inquiry into the KPMG scandal, seeking information about how the audit contract was awarded, but was told the company was "not aware of the whistleblower making specific claims in relation to Macquarie" and did not possess "any materials relevant".
Parliamentary officials also wrote to Hinchliffe, who did not respond.
On Thursday, Stevens said he was confident that the process of awarding the auditing contract had been a robust one, and that the company had "found the right balance between using Michelle's highly developed skills, which are very beneficial for the company and very beneficial in ensuring we have a good tender, and managing her potential contracts resulting from her previous employment, which were all fully disclosed and managed".
Macquarie shares ended down $1.18, or 0.5 per cent, at $253.75 on Thursday.
